findings.passage: You know, I think that’s racist to assume that people can’t get to the polls, you know, based upon those sort of, you know, markers. I personally have not run into anybody who’s had trouble doing that. And, you know, I work right here in Colchester. So I work with a diverse population and certainly have friends within the community. People show up with their license to get tickets to go to concerts. They show up with their license to get alcohol or cigarettes. They definitely have to show a license to get their medical marijuana. So, I mean, why not make it a priority for our voting?
findings.note: Answering a host's question about the argument that ID rules suppress turnout, she says she has not met anyone who had trouble getting ID, and says people already show a license for many other things. Same radio interview.

findings.passage: Well, I don’t love them at all. I think, you know, they’re fraught with opportunities for fraud. And I don’t, you know, the mail, the post office is in trouble too. I mean, my friend, I sent somebody a ballot, I mean, a petition, and they haven’t received it yet. It’s been like eight days, right? So, I mean, I’m not a big fan of the government efficiency issue. But when it comes to the mail-in ballots, I think I’m a no. And if you do need one, that should probably be built in there where you could get it if you’re disabled or having hardship or something along that lines. I’d also like to see Election Day as a national holiday so people could go.
findings.note: Asked by the host about absentee ballots and a federal bill that would limit them, she says she does not favor mail-in ballots, citing fraud risk and mail delays, but would allow one for disability or hardship. subjects: reasons allowed for a mail ballot
